title: Unified Multi-Provider SDK Patterns
summary: Build a thin adapter over the native Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google SDKs: normalize three different response shapes and stop signals, keep model ids and state policy in configuration, and treat OpenAI-compatible endpoints as a test harness because they silently drop guarantees.
objectives: Map the native request and response shapes of the Claude Messages API, the OpenAI Responses API, and the Gemini generateContent and Interactions APIs onto one internal contract.
Normalize stop signals and token usage so that truncation, refusal, pauses, and tool requests are never mistaken for a completed answer.
Explain what an OpenAI-compatible endpoint silently ignores when it fronts Claude or Gemini, and decide when such a layer is acceptable.
Keep model identifiers, API surface, and conversation-storage policy in configuration that a contract test verifies against the provider's current documentation.

sections.title: Three SDKs, three different ideas of a response
paragraphs: A portable client starts by admitting that the providers do not agree on what a response is. The Claude Messages API takes the system prompt as a top-level `system` parameter and prior turns in a `messages` array, and returns an assistant message whose `content` is an array of typed blocks such as `text` and `tool_use`. Anthropic describes the Messages API as usable for single queries or stateless multi-turn conversations: your application resends whatever history the model should see.

The OpenAI Responses API -- which OpenAI recommends for all new projects while Chat Completions remains supported -- returns an `output` array of Items. A `message` is one Item type; `reasoning`, `function_call`, and `function_call_output` are others, and OpenAI's own migration guide lists 'treating every output entry as a message' as a common error. The SDK's `output_text` helper joins the text for you, but only the Items tell you what else happened. Responses are stored by default unless you send `store: false`.

Google currently documents two Gemini surfaces. `generateContent` returns `candidates`, each with `content.parts` and a `finishReason`. The Interactions API returns an Interaction with a `status` and a `steps` timeline (`user_input`, `function_call`, `model_output`, and others), stores interactions by default (55 days on the paid tier, 1 day on the free tier), and is in beta: a `steps` array has already replaced an earlier `outputs` array in a breaking change. The same overview page recommends Interactions for new projects and tells production workloads to continue using `generateContent`. An adapter is how you make that choice once, in one place, and reverse it later without touching any caller.
sections.callout: The SDK is not the abstraction. The abstraction is the internal contract you write; each SDK sits behind an adapter that fills it.

sections.title: Normalize stop signals before you normalize text
paragraphs: The most expensive portability bug is a truncated or refused answer that flows downstream as if it were complete. Each provider signals this differently. Claude sets `stop_reason` to one of `end_turn`, `max_tokens`, `stop_sequence`, `tool_use`, `pause_turn`, `refusal`, or `model_context_window_exceeded`. The Responses API marks a cut-off answer with `status: "incomplete"` and an `incomplete_details.reason` such as `max_output_tokens`, and reports a safety refusal as a `refusal` content item instead of text. Gemini's `generateContent` reports a `finishReason` (`STOP` on a normal finish), and an Interaction waiting on your function result comes back with `status: "requires_action"`.

Map every native value into your own outcome, and make the mapping total: an unknown value becomes `other` and fails closed; it never defaults to `complete`. Keep the raw value as well, because 'why did this stop' is the first question in every incident review. `pause_turn` deserves its own outcome: Anthropic documents it as a paused long-running turn that you can send back as-is to let the model continue, which is neither success nor failure.

Usage needs the same treatment. Field names differ -- `usage.input_tokens` and `output_tokens` on Claude and on OpenAI Responses, `usageMetadata.promptTokenCount` and `candidatesTokenCount` on Gemini `generateContent` -- and so does their meaning. Anthropic notes that its counts will not match the visible content one-to-one and that total input is the sum of `input_tokens`, `cache_creation_input_tokens`, and `cache_read_input_tokens`; OpenAI notes that chaining with `previous_response_id` still bills the earlier input tokens. Store raw usage beside any normalized figure so a cost comparison can be audited.

Streaming multiplies the differences. Responses streaming emits typed server-sent events such as `response.output_text.delta`, `response.function_call_arguments.delta`, and `response.completed`; Gemini streams structured output as partial JSON strings that you concatenate; Claude's `stop_reason` is null in the `message_start` event and set later in the stream. A streaming adapter should emit the same internal events whatever the source, and declare an outcome only once the final stop signal has arrived.

sections.title: OpenAI-compatible endpoints are a test harness, not an abstraction
paragraphs: Both Anthropic and Google let the official OpenAI SDK talk to their models: change the base URL, the API key, and the model name. That looks like a free 'unified' client -- write against one SDK, swap three strings. Read what each owner says about it before shipping one.

Anthropic states that its compatibility layer is primarily intended to test and compare model capabilities and is not considered a long-term or production-ready solution for most use cases. On that layer the `strict` flag on function tools is ignored, so tool arguments are not guaranteed to follow your schema; `response_format` is ignored; `n` must be 1; `temperature` above 1 is capped at 1; every system or developer message is hoisted and concatenated into one leading system message; `choices[].message.refusal` is always empty; and prompt caching is unavailable. Most unsupported fields are silently ignored rather than rejected.

Google describes its OpenAI compatibility for Gemini as still in beta. It maps `reasoning_effort` onto Gemini thinking levels or budgets, exposes Gemini-only features through an `extra_body` field, and on image generation silently ignores parameters it does not list. Google itself recommends calling the Gemini API directly if you are not already using the OpenAI libraries.

The failure mode is quiet. A request that relied on `strict` or `response_format` still returns 200 and still parses most of the time, so nothing breaks until a malformed argument or a missing refusal signal reaches production. Use compatibility endpoints for what their owners say they are for -- side-by-side evaluation -- and send production traffic through native adapters. If you do keep one, write a contract test for every guarantee your code depends on and run it against that route, because the endpoint will not tell you it dropped one.
sections.callout: A compatibility endpoint that ignores a field returns the same HTTP 200 as one that honors it. Only a test that depends on the guarantee can tell the difference.

code.label: Guarantees are tests, not assumptions

sections.title: Model ids, API surface, and storage policy belong in configuration
paragraphs: Model identifiers change faster than code. As of 2026-09-11 the providers' own model pages list, among others, `claude-opus-5` and `claude-sonnet-5` on Anthropic (which states that every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot, including the dateless IDs used from the 4.6 generation on), `gpt-5.6-terra` on OpenAI (described as balancing intelligence and cost), and `gemini-3.8-flash` on Google (listed as stable). Put the id in configuration, record where and when it was verified, and fail startup or CI when it is missing -- never let an adapter fall back to a hardcoded default that nobody rereads. Anthropic's Models API returns `max_input_tokens`, `max_tokens`, and a `capabilities` object for each model, which a startup check can use.

Documentation can disagree with itself, which is exactly why the check belongs in code. Google's models page lists `gemini-3.8-flash` as stable and the Interactions guides use it in their examples, yet the supported-models table on the Interactions overview (as read on 2026-09-11) does not list it. A contract test that makes one real call per configured surface-and-model pair settles that for your project on the day you deploy; a comment in the source does not.

Treat state and retention as configuration too, because the defaults differ. The Claude Messages API keeps no conversation for you. The Responses API stores responses unless you send `store: false`, and OpenAI enforces `store: false` automatically for Zero Data Retention organizations. The Gemini Interactions API stores interactions by default; setting `store=false` also disables `previous_interaction_id` chaining and background execution, and when you do chain, `tools`, `system_instruction`, and `generation_config` are interaction-scoped and must be resent on every call. A unified client that exposes one `store` switch has to translate it per surface, and must refuse a combination the surface cannot honor rather than quietly keep data your policy said to discard.

activity.title: Build and probe a three-provider adapter
instructions: Define an internal result contract (outcome, joined text, tool calls with ids, raw stop value, raw usage) and write one adapter each for Claude Messages, OpenAI Responses, and one Gemini surface. State in one paragraph why you chose generateContent or Interactions for Gemini.
Write a total stop-signal mapping for each adapter and a unit test that feeds it every documented value plus one invented value; the invented value must not map to complete.

In a test environment, point the OpenAI SDK at Anthropic's compatibility endpoint and send one request that depends on strict tool arguments and one that depends on response_format. Record what the layer did with each.

Move every model id and storage setting into configuration with a verified-on date and source URL, and add a contract test that fails the build when a configured id is rejected or a storage setting cannot be honored on its surface.
evidence: Adapter code or a design, plus the stop-signal mapping table and its tests, including the invented-value case.
A short compatibility-layer finding that names each guarantee silently dropped and the native feature that replaces it.
A configuration file listing model ids, surfaces, and storage settings, each with a verified-on date and the URL it was verified against.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which provider difference would your adapter have hidden from you if you had normalized the text first and the stop signals second?

questions.prompt: A Claude response comes back with stop_reason "max_tokens". What should a portable adapter report?
choices: Complete, because text was returned
Truncated -- the output reached the token limit and may be incomplete
Refused
A tool request
questions.explanation: "max_tokens" means the requested limit or the model maximum was reached. Reporting it as complete lets a partial answer flow downstream.

questions.prompt: You call Claude through the OpenAI SDK compatibility endpoint with a function tool marked strict: true. What does Anthropic document about that flag?
choices: It is enforced exactly as it is on OpenAI
It is ignored, so tool arguments are not guaranteed to match the schema
It returns a 400 error
It reroutes the request to the native Messages API
questions.explanation: The compatibility layer ignores strict (and response_format). Guaranteed schema conformance requires structured outputs or strict tool use on the native Claude API.

questions.prompt: Why is "treat every item in response.output as a message" a bug in an OpenAI Responses adapter?
choices: output only ever contains one item
reasoning, function_call, and other Items are distinct types; only message Items carry the assistant text
Messages are returned in a separate choices field
Items are only returned when streaming
questions.explanation: OpenAI's migration guide lists this as a common error: Items are a union of types, and a message is only one of them.

questions.prompt: Your policy forbids server-side conversation storage features. Which statement about the default behavior is accurate?
choices: All three APIs keep nothing server-side by default
OpenAI Responses and Gemini Interactions store by default and need store set to false; Claude Messages relies on the history your application resends
Only Claude stores conversations by default
Storage is controlled by the model id
questions.explanation: Responses are stored unless store is false, Interactions are stored by default (and store=false disables previous_interaction_id chaining), and the Messages API is used for stateless multi-turn conversations.

questions.prompt: Google's Interactions overview recommends it for new projects and also says production workloads should continue to use generateContent. What is the adapter-level response?
choices: Choose Interactions because it is newer
Make the surface a configuration choice behind one internal contract, record the reason, and cover the chosen surface with contract tests
Use the OpenAI compatibility endpoint instead
Hardcode generateContent and remove the adapter
questions.explanation: Keeping the surface behind an adapter makes the choice reversible; the beta Interactions API has already had one breaking schema change, steps replacing outputs.
